nameStory: The name 'mouse-ear' comes from the shape of this little plant's leaves, which are small, rounded, and fuzzy just like a mouse's ear! The 'dwarf' part refers to its tiny stature - this is one of the smallest members of the mouse-ear chickweed family. Early botanists had quite an imagination when it came to seeing animal parts in plant shapes!
description: Dwarf mouse-ear is a tiny annual plant that grows only 2-8 inches tall, making it easy to overlook among other spring wildflowers. This petite member of the pink family produces small white flowers with deeply notched petals that bloom from March through May. The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture and grows close to the ground in a low, spreading manner. Despite being native to Europe, it has quietly made its way to a few spots in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with 5 deeply split petals that are shorter than or equal to the green sepals beneath them. Each petal is notched about a quarter of the way down, giving them a heart-shaped appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves that feel soft and fuzzy to the touch, arranged in pairs along the stem. They're pale green and covered in fine hairs that give them a velvety texture reminiscent of a mouse's ear.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely small plant, typically under 8 inches tall, growing in a low, mat-like spread close to the ground. The whole plant has a delicate, almost fragile appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Seed pods on stalks that stick out at an angle from the stem, often bending over at the tip like tiny curved fingers. The pods split open to release small seeds.

habitat: Look for dwarf mouse-ear in disturbed soils, sandy areas, and open spaces with poor, well-drained ground. In New England, it's extremely rare and has been found in coastal areas and waste places. It prefers spots where larger plants haven't crowded it out, thriving in the kind of thin, sandy soil that many other plants avoid.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for dwarf mouse-ear, with its tiny white flowers blooming from March through May. The entire fuzzy plant is most visible and identifiable during its brief flowering period.
seasonality.summer: Flowering ends and the plant produces its angled seed pods before often disappearing entirely. By midsummer, annual plants may have completed their life cycle.
seasonality.fall: As an annual, most plants have died back by fall, leaving only seeds to survive the winter and start the cycle again next spring.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible. Seeds lie dormant in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Despite being called 'European chickweed,' dwarf mouse-ear is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice by naturalists - making it more elusive than some endangered species! You're more likely to see a wild moose than this tiny European immigrant.
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other mouse-ear chickweeds, but dwarf mouse-ear's tiny size and petals that are shorter than the sepals help distinguish it. Remember: if the white petals seem hidden behind green sepals on a plant smaller than your palm, you might have found the dwarf species.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'chickweed' fool you into thinking this is the same as common chickweed (Stellaria media) that grows in everyone's yard. The mouse-ear chickweeds belong to a different genus entirely, though they're in the same pink family and share that characteristic deeply-split petal look.
compareHints: Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals. Common mouse-ear chickweed is much larger and more robust, while snow-in-summer is a garden escape with showier, longer petals. The angled, often bent-over seed stalks are also more pronounced in dwarf mouse-ear than in its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England.
Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance.
Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs.
American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
